18.0.big: Evolution is the one theme that ties all of biology together: every living thing descends from a common ancestor, and evolution is still happening.
points: Example: a green sea slug steals photosynthesis genes from the algae it eats (horizontal gene transfer), so it can photosynthesize like a plant.

18.1.big: Natural selection: individuals with helpful, inherited traits survive and reproduce more, so those traits become more common over generations.
points: Darwin and Wallace came up with natural selection independently. Darwin's clues included Galápagos finch beaks. Lamarck's wrong idea was inheritance of acquired characteristics (use a body part and your kids get a better one).
Darwin's three ingredients: traits are inherited, more offspring are born than can survive (competition), and offspring vary. Result: the better-suited leave more offspring.
Variation must be genetic to matter. It comes from mutation (the only source of brand-new alleles) and sexual reproduction (shuffles them).
An adaptation is a heritable trait that helps survival and reproduction in the current environment. Change the environment and the best trait can change.
Divergent evolution: one ancestor, many different forms (human arm, whale flipper). Convergent evolution: unrelated species evolve similar solutions (bat and insect wings).

Evidence: fossils, homologous structures (same bones, different jobs), vestigial structures (whale hip bones, flightless bird wings), embryos (all vertebrate embryos have gill slits and tails), biogeography (Australia's marsupials), and DNA similarity.
Evolution is happening now: bacteria becoming antibiotic-resistant.

Myths to bust: "just a theory" (a scientific theory is a heavily tested explanation, not a guess); individuals don't evolve, populations do; evolution doesn't explain the origin of life; evolution has no goal; resistance genes were already there before the antibiotic came.
18.1.tip: Homologous = same ancestor (same bones). Analogous/convergent = same job, different ancestors.

18.2.big: A species is a group that can interbreed and make fertile, viable offspring. Speciation happens when populations become reproductively isolated.
points: Looks can fool you: poodles and cocker spaniels are one species. Bald eagles and African fish eagles are two. A hybrid between species is usually infertile.

Allopatric speciation ("other homeland"): a geographic barrier splits the population. It happens by dispersal (some members move away) or vicariance (a river, lake or valley forms and divides them). Example: northern vs. Mexican spotted owls.
Adaptive radiation: one founder species spreads into many niches and becomes many species. Examples: Hawaiian honeycreepers, Darwin's finches.

Sympatric speciation ("same homeland"): no barrier. Often by polyploidy (extra full sets of chromosomes), mostly in plants. Autopolyploid = extra sets from its own species. Allopolyploid = sets from two species (wheat, cotton, tobacco). Aneuploidy = one chromosome too many or too few.

Prezygotic barriers (before fertilization): temporal (breed at different times), habitat, behavioral (firefly flash patterns), mechanical (parts don't fit), gametic (egg and sperm don't fuse), and different pollinators.
Postzygotic barriers (after fertilization): hybrid inviability (embryo dies) and hybrid sterility (mule).
18.2.tip: Pre = before the zygote (they never make a baby). Post = a baby is made but it dies or is sterile.

18.3.big: After two species split, they may meet again. And speciation can be slow and steady or happen in sudden bursts.
points: A hybrid zone is where two related species still meet and make hybrids. Three outcomes:

Reinforcement: hybrids are less fit, so barriers get stronger and the species keep diverging. Fusion: barriers weaken and the two become one species again. Stability: hybrids keep being made with no net change.
Gradual speciation model: small changes over long periods. Fossils show many in-between forms.
Punctuated equilibrium: fast change (often a small group cut off by sudden environmental change), then long periods of little change.
The main thing that changes the speed of speciation is the environment.

1.why: Both independently came up with natural selection.

2.why: False: more offspring are born than can survive, so there is always competition for resources.

3.why: An adaptation must be heritable and help the organism survive and reproduce.

4.why: Webbed feet are inherited and help ducks swim. Better nutrition isn't inherited.

5.why: Divergent = groups evolve in different directions from a common point.

6.why: Worms and snakes are unrelated but both evolved to move without legs: convergent.

7.why: Homologous = similar structures because of a common ancestor.

8.why: Whale hind leg bones and cactus leaves don't do their original job anymore: vestigial.

9.why: Evolution explains how life changes, but it doesn't try to explain how life began.

10.why: The resistance gene was already there. The antibiotic kills the others, so the gene becomes more common.

11.why: Species = they interbreed and make viable, fertile offspring.

12.why: Species are defined by whether they can reproduce together, so scientists look at reproductive barriers.

13.why: Mutation makes new alleles, and sexual reproduction shuffles them.

14.why: With no genetic variation, there's nothing for selection to act on, so speciation can't happen.

15.why: Reproductive organs not fitting stops mating before fertilization, so it's prezygotic, not postzygotic.

16.why: Different pollinators mean pollen never reaches the other flower. No zygote forms: prezygotic.

17.why: A new lake physically splits the population, which is geographic separation.

18.why: The difference is the source: auto = its own species, allo = two different species.

19.why: Adaptive radiation = many new species from one parent species.

20.why: Empty niches, isolated habitats and few competitors all help. Genetic drift isn't what drives it.

21.why: In a hybrid zone they keep reproducing together and making hybrids.

22.why: Reinforcement = hybrids do poorly, so barriers strengthen.

23.why: False: punctuated equilibrium usually happens in a small population after a sudden change, not a large one in a stable environment.

24.why: Speciation needs gene flow to stop. Ongoing gene flow wouldn't fit.

25.why: Two scientists reaching the same conclusion independently makes that conclusion more credible.

26.why: If faster running is genetic and helps survival and reproduction, natural selection favors it.

27.why: Insects and birds both fly with wings built from very different parts: convergent evolution from similar pressures.

28.why: Vestigial parts are leftovers from a shared ancestor, showing groups evolved from a common point.

29.why: On land, sperm can't swim through water and pollen-style scattering wouldn't work, so humans evolved internal fertilization: sperm are delivered inside the body, where the egg stays moist and protected. The embryo also develops inside the mother (placenta), protected from drying out.

30.why: No. A unique gene can appear by mutation or gene duplication and then change over time. The rest of our genome, the universal genetic code, and shared genes with other species still show a common ancestor.

31.why: Where malaria is common, people with the mutation would have higher fitness because they survive malaria more often, even though they risk anemia. So the allele would become more common there (like sickle-cell).

32.why: Scientific theory = thoroughly tested explanation. Everyday "theory" = a guess.

33.why: Evolution is measured as change in species and populations, so the species is the unit you track.

34.why: A mutation in fur (a body cell) isn't in the sperm or egg, so it can't be passed on.

35.why: Barriers stop interbreeding, so there's no gene flow, and the populations stay separate species.

36.why: Interbreeding dropped to zero by about 20 years, which suggests they're reproductively isolated. But to be sure they're new species, you'd test whether they can still make fertile offspring if brought together. If they can't, they're separate species.

37.why: Allopatric is more common because a physical barrier completely stops gene flow.

38.why: One finch species spread to different islands, and different foods selected for different beak shapes.

39.why: If hybrids are more fit, interbreeding continues and the two species fuse into one.

40.why: The number of frog lineages shoots up recently after a long flat stretch: a sudden jump (punctuated equilibrium) that's still going.

41.why: Less-fit hybrids lead to reinforcement, so the species keep diverging.

42.why: The moths that matched the bark survived and reproduced more: differential reproduction.

43.why: Clean, light bark means dark moths stand out again, so light moths increase and dark moths decrease.

44.why: Large-scale (macro) evolution means something truly new: the moth develops a new adaptation, not just swapping between existing forms.

45.why: Many of the same genes (in the same order) appear in both, so humans and mice share some genes.

46.why: Nearby plants being related, even in different climates, fits descent with modification from local ancestors.

47.why: A reptile with feathers is an in-between form, showing reptiles and birds share a common ancestor.

48.why: Penicillin-resistant Staph appeared within decades. That's evolution happening now.

49.why: The apes' extra chromosome pair lines up with human chromosome 2, so two ape chromosomes fused in humans. The common ancestor had 48.

50.why: The map shows marsupials moving from the Americas through Antarctica to Australia, so Antarctica should have marsupial fossils.

51.why: Small changes in the embryo have magnified effects on the adult, often deadly, so these genes stay the same.

52.why: Same ancestor, but the whale's flipper changed shape as an adaptation to water.

53.why: Dinosaurs started before Pangaea broke up, so their fossils should be on many continents.

54.why: With DDT everywhere, flies carrying the resistance allele survived and reproduced more, so the allele rose from 0% to 40%.

55.why: Even where the ulna is vestigial, it's still there, so these mammals and humans share an ancestor that had an ulna.

56.why: The drug killed the non-resistant viruses, and the resistant ones multiplied: natural selection happening right now.

57.why: "Fittest" means best at surviving and reproducing, not strongest or biggest.

58.why: In dish B, all seedlings got the same light, yet some were yellow and some green. That points to genes.

59.why: About 5 or 6 yellow seedlings showed up whether in light or dark, so their germination is unaffected by light.

60.why: Yellow seedlings can't photosynthesize, so once their seed food runs out, none survive in either dish.

61.why: Few, frail hybrids = a postzygotic barrier, which is strong evidence they're separate species.

62.why: The Devonian extinction hit marine life (reefs, corals, brachiopods, bivalves), so search sediment for marine fossils.

63.why: Test directly whether they can cross and make fertile offspring, and look for fertile hybrids in between.

64.why: If they can cross and make fertile offspring, they're still one species.

65.why: Environment changes, then poorly adapted individuals die more, then the well-adapted leave more offspring, then gene frequencies change, then phenotypes shift.

66.why: More survived, so there was more food or less predation. Less selection means more variation survives.

67.why: Big-beaked birds survive and reproduce more, so future generations have more big beaks. Individual beaks don't grow.

68.why: Being a separate species means reproductive isolation.

69.why: Gradual = many in-between forms. Punctuated = forms stay the same for many layers, then suddenly change.

71.why: Poor hybrids mean selection favors not mating with the other species: prezygotic barriers strengthen (reinforcement).
